question: Bisphosphonates reduce bone resorption primarily by which mechanism, and what is their most serious rare long-term adverse effect?

answers.text: Activating osteoblasts via PTH receptor agonism; osteosarcoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That describes teriparatide (anabolic), not bisphosphonates. Bisphosphonates are anti-resorptive, not anabolic.

answers.text: Inhibiting osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase; osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit FPP synthase in the mevalonate pathway, impairing osteoclast function. ONJ (and atypical femoral fractures) are recognised rare serious adverse effects.
RANK-L blockade describes denosumab, not bisphosphonates. Bisphosphonates act intracellularly on osteoclasts.
Bisphosphonates do not act via calcitonin. Calcitonin itself is a separate anti-resorptive agent with modest efficacy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase → impaired osteoclast cytoskeleton → reduced bone resorption. Rare serious ADRs: ONJ and atypical subtrochanteric fractures.
Excellent! Remembering the FPP synthase mechanism explains why nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates are more potent than first-generation agents.
